title: LARGE and SMALL: the nth highest

screens.prompt: Put the second-best time in the team into C2, keeping the list unsorted.

hints.syntax: LARGE takes the range, then which one you want: =LARGE(B2:B6,2).
hints.func-large: MAX gives the top time only. The second one needs a function that counts in from the top.
hints.require-ref: Point at the column of times instead of listing them inside the formula.
hints.value: The 2 is a position, not a row number. The highest time is 61, so the second highest is 58.
hints.error: #NUM! means the position is outside the list: it appears when the second argument is 0 or larger than the count.

reject.why: the highest time, 61, which is not the second highest
counts in from the bottom, so it returns 55
one argument only — LARGE needs to be told which one
the range starts at B3, so the fastest swimmer is left out of the count
the best time, 61, rather than the one after it
division by zero, so the cell holds #DIV/0!
the missing comma means the arguments never separate

screens.prompt: Put the second-cheapest quote into C2 without re-sorting the table.

hints.syntax: SMALL is LARGE counted from the other end: =SMALL(B2:B6,2).
hints.func-small: MIN returns the cheapest quote and stops there. The next one up needs SMALL.
hints.require-ref: Read the quotes from B2:B6, so the numbers live in one place.
hints.value: 35 is the cheapest. The second cheapest is 38, which is what the 2 asks for.
hints.error: #VALUE! appears when the first argument holds text, as a column of quote codes would.

reject.why: the cheapest quote, 35, rather than the one after it
counts in from the top, so it returns 47
the first quote is outside the range, so the count starts one place too high
the cheapest quote, 35, not the second cheapest
the fourth cheapest, 47, which is two places too far up the list
division by zero, so the cell holds #DIV/0!
the missing comma leaves two arguments jammed into one

docs.explain:
LARGE returns the value at a given position counted from the top of the list, and SMALL counts the same way from the bottom. The second argument is a rank, so 1 is the highest and 2 the one after it. Nothing is sorted: the sheet keeps its rows and the answer sits wherever the formula is written.

Here the times run 58, 61, 55, 57 and 50, so the highest is 61 and the second highest is 58. The quote column works the other way: 35 is the cheapest and 38 the next one up, which is what SMALL with a 2 returns.

The position is the usual mistake, because 2 looks like a row number. A position of 0, or one past the end of the list, returns #NUM! where a value should be. A headline built on LARGE needs a guard when the list can shrink.

errors.text: The position is 0 or larger than the count of values, and LARGE has no such place in the order.
The first argument holds text rather than a block of numbers, and text has no order to count through.
LARGE on a list of times returns the slowest and SMALL the fastest, so the number is right and the label above it is wrong.

docs.atWork: A team sheet naming the second-best time, and a tender list tracking the second-cheapest quote, both without re-sorting the table.
docs.outcome: Pick the nth value in an unsorted list instead of sorting it to read one number.
docs.teaches: LARGE and SMALL with a position argument
docs.dataset: Swim times and five supplier quotes

seo.title: LARGE and SMALL in Excel: the nth value
seo.description: LARGE counts in from the top of an unsorted list and SMALL from the bottom, so the second argument is a position, not a row number. No sort needed.
